1359.title: Learning from one stream
1359.hook: each stream keeps some treasure well
1359.howItsDone: Some Sikhs learn from a stream other than their own: practicing gatka with Nihangs, learning pronunciation through taksal teaching, studying raga kirtan at gurmat sangeet schools, or joining early-morning programs in Western sangats.

segments.voice: Yesterday, visiting another stream: shoes off, head covered, cupped hands for karah prashad. Your line was courtesy is enough.

A grandmother keeps the family's pickle recipe. An uncle remembers which villages the family came from. A cousin is the only one who still plays the harmonium properly. Nobody holds everything. Lose one of them and something goes quiet in the family. The panth works a bit like that. Over this block, stream after stream turned out to be guarding something particular. Today asks what each one keeps, and what anyone might borrow.
screen: `A RECIPE, A MAP, A HARMONIUM.` → `NOBODY HOLDS EVERYTHING.` → `WHAT DOES EACH STREAM KEEP?`

segments.voice: Walk back through the streams and look for the treasure each keeps well. The Nihangs keep the old warrior dress, the martial art of gatka, and a playful, defiant way of speaking. The taksals keep pronunciation: students learn to read Gurbani slowly, syllable by syllable, so that the Guru's words come out whole. The Nirmalas keep learning, scholars reading widely and explaining the Granth. The Udasis keep a life of renunciation and care for shrines. The Namdharis keep simplicity, white dress, and kirtan sung in the old ragas. The gurmat sangeet schools keep those ragas alive for everyone. Sikh Dharma sangats in the West keep early-morning practice, and some Western sangats explain things in English for newcomers. The rababis kept music at the Harmandir, and the dhadis keep history in the voice. Not one of these is the whole panth. Each keeps a corner of the house well lit. Gurbani gives an image for this. In Raag Suhi, around Ang 765, Guru Nanak speaks of a box of virtues: if someone has one, open it and enjoy its fragrance; and if a friend has virtues, become partners in them, and leave faults behind. That's the posture of learning from a stream. You don't have to join it, or agree with it on everything. You can borrow its fragrance: a slower way of reading, an earlier hour, a raga, a straighter back. The streams lose nothing by sharing. That's how a fragrance works.

1360.title: One Guru, many sangats
1360.hook: the variety of the panth is its breadth, not its weakness
1360.howItsDone: Sikhs of many streams gather in their own sangats around the same Guru Granth Sahib, and Sohila, the night prayer with its line on the one light in everyone, is recited before sleep.

segments.voice: Yesterday, learning from one stream: a box of virtues, opened and shared. Your line was each keeps a treasure.

Someone who listened to this whole block might come away with a worry. Blue-robed Nihangs and white-clad Namdharis. Strict ragas and simple tunes. Meat on one plate, none on another. Arguments over a calendar, a book, the five at the bowl. Isn't a faith with this many streams coming apart at the seams? It's a fair question, and an honest one. Outsiders ask it, and so, sometimes, do Sikhs themselves. Today offers another way to see the same picture.
screen: `SO MANY STREAMS.` → `IS IT COMING APART?` → `ANOTHER WAY TO SEE IT.`

segments.voice: Start with what doesn't vary. The Sikh streams this block visited bow to the same Guru Granth Sahib, and the Mool Mantar at its opening names one Creator for all of them. So the sangats are many, and the Guru is one. Now look at the variety again, from the center outward. A banyan tree drops roots from its branches until a single tree looks like a grove. Its width isn't a sign of trouble; it's how the tree holds more shade. The panth has spread across villages and cities, castes and continents, warriors and scholars and singers, and each has taken the same Word into a different life. Gurbani gives the reason the spread doesn't scatter it. In Sohila, the night prayer, Guru Nanak says on Ang 13, here in paraphrase: the one light is in everyone, and that light is the One; by its shining, everyone is lit. If the same light is in each sangat, then many sangats is simply the light, showing up in many rooms. That doesn't make every disagreement easy; this block has been honest that some are hard. But breadth means a Sikh who struggles in one sangat can find another under the same Guru. It means a newcomer in Texas and an elder in Amritsar can open the same page. It means the panth can carry music and martial art, study and service, quiet and loud, without needing them all in one person.

Then widen it to the people unlike you who make your world bigger, and if you pray, thank Waheguru for the one light in all of them.

1361.title: The streams close
1361.hook: orders, schools, communities, places and music
1361.tomorrow: Names of God in the Granth
1361.howItsDone: The Sikh panth lives in many streams, including orders, schools, communities, historic places and musical traditions, and Sikhs visit gurdwaras and gatherings beyond their own, with the Guru Granth Sahib at the center of the Sikh streams.

segments.voice: Yesterday, one Guru, many sangats: one light, showing up in many rooms. Your line was breadth, not weakness.

From high on a hill, a river delta doesn't look like one river. It looks like a hand of silver fingers, braiding apart and back together on the way to the sea. Stand on the bank of any one channel and you'd swear it was the only one. Go up the hill and you see the whole shape. This block has been a walk along the channels of the Sikh panth. Today is the view from the hill, before the path turns to Sikh thought.
screen: `A DELTA FROM THE HILL.` → `ONE CHANNEL LOOKS LIKE THE RIVER.` → `TODAY, THE WHOLE SHAPE.`

segments.voice: Here's the shape. First, the orders: Udasis in renunciation, Nirmalas in learning, Sevapanthis in service, and the Nihang dals in blue. Then the schools: the Damdami Taksal and its careful pronunciation, the Akhand Kirtani Jatha and its nights of kirtan, the Nanaksar tradition. Then the communities: Namdharis in white, Baba Dayal's Nirankaris, Sikh Dharma in the West, Sindhi devotees of Nanak, Sikligar, Lubana and Vanjara Sikhs, the Sikhs of Assam, Mazhabi Sikhs, craftsmen and builders, and the Ravidassia community with its own story. Then the places: the Harmandir's day and the Akal Takht, Delhi's gurdwaras, Nankana and Kartarpur, Panja Sahib, Anandpur, Fatehgarh, Muktsar, Goindval, Khadur, Tarn Taran, Baba Bakala, Kiratpur, snowy Hemkunt, and gurdwaras abroad. Then the music and the arts: rababis, ragas and simple tunes, dhadis, kavishri, katha, gurmat sangeet, painting, architecture, phulkari. And last, the studies, the open questions, and one Granth at the center of them all. Guru Nanak has an image for streams. In the Japji, on Ang 5, he says, here in paraphrase, that rivers and streams flow into the ocean, yet cannot know how vast it is. The streams of the panth are like that. Each pours into something larger than itself, and none of them holds all of it. That's a fitting place to turn from the people of the panth to its thought. Tomorrow the path begins with the names of God in the Granth.

1362.title: Names of God in the Granth
1362.word: Names of God in the Granth
1362.hook: Waheguru, Ram, Hari, Gobind, Allah, Khuda, Prabh, Akal: the Granth uses many
1362.howItsDone: In gurdwaras the Guru Granth Sahib is read aloud, and listeners hear the One called by many names, among them Hari, Ram, Gobind, Prabh, Allah and Khuda, all read as names of the same One.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the streams closed: orders, schools, communities, places and music, none of them holding all of it. Your line: many streams. Today the path turns from the people of the panth to its thought.

What is God's name? It's a question a child might ask in the back of a gurdwara. Sit through a morning of reading from the Guru Granth Sahib with that question in your pocket, and the answer keeps changing. One hymn says Hari. The next says Ram. Then Gobind, then Prabh, the Lord. In some hymns the word is Allah, or Khuda. One book, read from one cloth-covered stand, calls on the One by name after name. A new part of the year starts here: Sikh thought, the big ideas underneath the history.
screen: `WHAT IS GOD'S NAME?` → `HARI, RAM, GOBIND, ALLAH, KHUDA.` → `A NEW PART: SIKH THOUGHT.`

segments.voice: Start with the pages. The Granth gathers hymns from the Gurus and from other saints, and they reach for the language listeners already used. So the One is Hari and Ram and Gobind, names from the devotional songs people knew, and also Allah and Khuda, words their Muslim neighbors prayed with. The Granth's opening line adds names of its own: Akal Murat, the Timeless Form, and the creator without fear and without hate. Why so many? Guru Arjan answers in a hymn in Raag Maru. In paraphrase: my tongue speaks the names that describe what You have done, but True Name is Your name from before everything. Our names are names of deeds: the one who sustains, who protects, who made the world. Each catches one thing the One does. None catches the One. That shapes how a name is heard. When Sikhs read Ram in the Granth, they read it as the One present in everything, not one figure from one story. The names point past themselves. And Sikh readers draw a plain lesson from a book that sets Allah beside Hari: nobody owns the word for God, and no name has to be defended against another. A name is a door, not a fence. One name sits at the center of Sikh daily prayer, and that's tomorrow. But the Granth keeps the crowd. Many names.

1363.title: The name Waheguru
1363.hook: the name used by the Bhatts in their verses praising the Gurus (Swayye, ang 1402)
1363.howItsDone: Sikhs repeat Waheguru in simran, alone or together, and use it in the greeting Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki fateh; congregations often say it aloud at the end of a reading.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the names of God in the Granth: Hari, Ram, Gobind, Allah, Khuda and more. Your line: many names. Today, the one at the center.

Wah. A sound people make without deciding to. A sunset over the fields. A baby's first step. A friend's voice on the phone after years. Now set that sound right in front of the word Guru. Waheguru. It was the very first word on this path, back on day one. It's the name Sikhs repeat in simran, the word in the greeting Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki fateh, the name a congregation says together as a reading ends. And in the Granth itself it turns up somewhere a newcomer might not look: near the end of the book, in the voices of poets.
screen: `WAH: THE SOUND OF WONDER.` → `WAH + GURU.` → `IN THE VOICES OF POETS.`

segments.voice: Close to the end of the Guru Granth Sahib come the Swayye of the Bhatts, verses by bards who praised the Gurus. Tradition remembers them as poets who came to the Guru's court and sang what they saw, and their verses sit in the same scripture as the Gurus' own hymns. Around Ang fourteen hundred and two, in a verse praising Guru Ram Das, a Bhatt named Gayand breaks again and again into one cry: Waheguru, Waheguru, Waheguru. It reads less like a definition than like someone who can't stop saying it. Sikhs explain the name as wonder joined to Guru: wah, the cry of astonishment, and Guru, the one who brings light and teaching. Something like wonderful Lord. Notice what kind of name that is. Yesterday, Guru Arjan said our names describe God's deeds. Waheguru doesn't describe a deed. It describes what happens to the one who notices. It's mostly a gasp. From a bard's song it became the center of daily life. Sikhs repeat it in simran, slowly or quickly, aloud or under the breath, and call it gurmantar, the Guru's own word to repeat. A name that began as praise is now said in kitchens, cars and hospital rooms. Wonderful Lord.

The name Waheguru. Wonder joined to Guru: the name the Bhatts cried out in their verses, and the name Sikhs repeat in simran today. Today's word.

1364.title: With qualities, without
1364.hook: the One is both beyond all qualities and present in every quality
1364.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of the One as nirgun, beyond all qualities, and sargun, present in every form, and Sukhmani Sahib, which holds both together, is recited by Sikhs at home and in gurdwaras.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the name Waheguru: wah, the cry of wonder, joined to Guru. Your line: wonderful lord.

Is God far off, or right here? Put that to a room of people and the answers tend to split. Lean too far one way, and God is a distance with no one in it. Lean too far the other, and God shrinks to a figure you could fit in a picture frame. Sikh scripture doesn't make anyone pick. It holds both answers in one breath, with two words that sound almost like twins. Today's word is the first of them.
screen: `FAR OFF, OR RIGHT HERE?` → `NO NEED TO PICK.` → `TWO WORDS, ALMOST TWINS.`

segments.voice: Nirgun first. In the Granth's language, gun means a quality, a trait, the kind of thing you'd list to describe someone. Nirgun is the One without qualities: beyond every description, past anything we could name, measure or picture. No shape, no color, no edge where it stops. Then its twin, sargun: the One with qualities, present in every form there is, in the river and the mountain, in the stranger at the bus stop, in the patience of an old woman cooking for the langar. In Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan's long hymn of peace, one line holds both. In paraphrase: the One is without qualities, and the One is with qualities too. Not two gods, a far one and a near one taking turns. One, both ways at once. Sikh teachers sometimes use the picture of the ocean and its waves: the ocean has no single shape, and every wave is still the ocean. Why does it matter on an ordinary afternoon? If the One were only beyond, you'd have to leave the world to find it. If the One were only here, it would shrink to whatever you happened to like. Together, nirgun and sargun keep both doors open: awe at what no one can hold, and tenderness toward what is right in front of you. Vast and close.
screen: `NIRGUN: BEYOND EVERY QUALITY.` · `SARGUN: PRESENT IN EVERY FORM.` · `ONE, BOTH WAYS AT ONCE.` · `AWE AND TENDERNESS TOGETHER.` · then, large: `VAST AND CLOSE.`

segments.voice: First think of the biggest thing you can, a mountain range, a desert, everyone who has ever lived, and let it be too big to hold. Then bring your attention to something small and near: your own hand, a sound in the room, the next breath. If you pray, hold both as one; if not, just notice the shift from vast to close, and back.
Nirgun. The One without qualities, beyond every description, held together with sargun, the One present in every form. Today's word.
Your line: vast and close. Beyond every word, and in everything words touch. Rest well.

1365.title: The sky is the tray
1365.carry: beyond every sky, and the light within all
1365.howItsDone: Sikhs recite Sohila at night, which includes Guru Nanak's aarti picturing the sky as the tray of lamps and the light in everything as the One's light; Guru Nanak's aarti is also sung as kirtan in the evening.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nirgun and its twin, sargun: the One beyond every quality and present in every form. Your line: vast and close.

Dusk, and in a temple in Guru Nanak's world, priests lift trays: little lamps, flowers, incense, a pearl or two, waved in circles before an image. It's called aarti, a worship of light. Tradition tells of Guru Nanak watching a ceremony like this, then stepping outside and singing his own. His tray was much bigger. You met that hymn in year two. Sikhs still sing it at the end of the day, and it holds today's idea, because in one hymn it goes as far out as a hymn can go, and then as far in.
screen: `LAMPS ON A TRAY, AT DUSK.` → `GURU NANAK SINGS HIS OWN.` → `AS FAR OUT, THEN AS FAR IN.`

segments.voice: The hymn opens, in paraphrase: the sky is the tray, the sun and moon are the lamps, the stars are the pearls. The breeze is the incense, the wind is the fan, and all the forests are flowers. The whole universe is already doing aarti, and no temple tray could hold it. That's beyond: the One past every size we can manage. The English word is transcendent. Then the hymn turns, again in paraphrase: in everything there is a light, and that light is You. By that light, everything is lit. Five days ago that line held the many sangats together. Here it sits where Guru Nanak placed it, right after the sky-sized tray, in Sohila, the bedtime prayer. That's within: the One inside every living thing. The English word is immanent. The turn is the point. Guru Nanak doesn't sing one hymn for the stars and another for the heart. He sings one, and you can't keep one half and drop the other. Look back at the week: many sangats under one Guru, many streams, many names, the name Waheguru, nirgun and sargun. Each day circled the same shape. Many, and one. This hymn says it under an open sky. Beyond and within.
screen: `THE SKY IS THE TRAY.` · `IN EVERYTHING, A LIGHT.` · `ONE HYMN, NOT TWO.` · `THE WEEK: MANY, AND ONE.` · then, large: `BEYOND AND WITHIN.`

segments.voice: Look up, out a window or in your mind: the sky as a tray, the sun or moon as a lamp, the moving air as incense, and let it be huge. Then close your eyes and turn the same attention inward, to the warmth of your own breath. Same attention, different direction. If you pray, say or listen to Sohila tonight, where this hymn sits.
Beyond and within. Transcendent and immanent at once: the One past every size, and the light inside every living thing, held in one hymn. Today's word.
Your line: beyond every sky, and the light within all. One hymn, sung under the whole sky. That's the week.
